title: Vable's Matthew Dickinson on Current Awareness in the Age of GenAI
author: Matthew Dickinson

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: Shaver does not assess whether product expansion has translated into realised value, renewal economics or workflow fit. Instead, she reframes the issue around generative AI’s prospective productivity benefits for smaller and mid-sized firms and the need for education and vendor exposure to encourage adoption; the claimed gains remain unmeasured.
qs: We also know that they stand to gain the most from generative AI and efforts to automate and increase productivity because it can be a real game changer for them.

We’ve partnered with some of the most interesting vendors for mid-size firms who present speed demos during the events so that firms can see the technology that’s out there and learn what some of their competitors are using and what they may be interested in using themselves.

st.an: Dickinson supports lawyer-in-the-loop augmentation, judgment and responsibility, which aligns with the cluster’s supervision themes. st.an: Dickinson accepts selective, practical current awareness and materially develops the cluster’s filtering proposition with operational requirements: human editorial review, audience-sensitive quality thresholds, source diversity, provenance and publisher trust. He offers product priorities and proposed safeguards rather than measured performance evidence.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Dickinson accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model and develops it through a concrete current-awareness use case. He assigns final judgment and accountability to lawyers while proposing audience-specific accuracy thresholds, editorial review and controlled source inputs for higher-stakes outputs.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Dickinson supports the cluster’s supervised, human-accountable model of AI adoption and its view that workflow and organisational change—not tool access alone—constrain implementation. His contribution is narrower than the cluster: it focuses on current-awareness workflows and does not substantively address pricing, buyer incentives, staffing succession or market-wide delivery redesign.

And the solutions then need to be adopted by law firms, and there will be impact workflows and ways of working.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: Dickinson directly supports the cluster’s principal claim that AI’s benefits depend on continued human control. His optimism is explicitly conditional on people retaining responsibility for creativity and other important choices; he offers a recommendation rather than empirical evidence.
qs: But I think it is something positive and the only caveat to all of that is, as I said earlier, we do need to stay in charge.
No delegation of the important things, that creativity or things which are important to us in how we go from A to B.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: Dickinson supports the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition in the narrow context of current-awareness services: effective delivery depends on staffing, resources, personalisation and usable workflows, not technology alone. However, he provides no measured outcomes, task-specific evaluation or account of how GenAI would reliably overcome these constraints.
qs: And this has been a challenge, of course, to administrators, the information specialists, the librarians, due to lack of technology, resources, people, to really completely sort of customize the output for individuals’ needs and interests.
AI,  relying upon Boolean searching and challenges and trying to create a really intuitive service for lawyers that doesn’t involve complex Boolean queries has been challenging in itself.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: Dickinson directly supports selective augmentation: AI should generate ideas and preliminary material, while lawyers make the final judgment and remain responsible for outputs and client communication. His position reinforces the cluster’s central copilot framing, though it offers personal workflow experience rather than empirical evidence about productivity, verification costs or staffing effects.

st.an: Shaver supports the cluster’s core proposition by presenting generative AI adoption as requiring segment-specific education and structured exposure to relevant vendors, particularly for underserved smaller and mid-sized firms. Her productivity claims are promotional and anecdotal rather than evidence of measured outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.

kp.k: Current awareness shifts from article delivery to contextual insights
kp.d: Dickinson argues that GenAI has raised lawyers' expectations beyond emailed article lists: they now expect relevance assessment and implications without having to read everything themselves. Earlier manual curation, Boolean searching and limited staffing made individualisation across hundreds or thousands of lawyers difficult. He illustrates the intended change with a client data-breach alert that supplies a summary, potential implications and other firm colleagues who should know; this is a proposed workflow, not a demonstrated outcome.
qs: So imagine really supporting hundreds if not thousands of lawyers in multiple offices and even understanding their individual needs and trying to deliver a very precise individual service to them.
They don’t want to have to read them to determine what is of relevance and then to work out what to do with that information.
And here’s the summary. Here’s the potential implications. And let’s go even further and actually here’s who else in the firm should know about this.

kp.k: Integration enables proactive, role-specific information delivery
kp.d: Dickinson anticipates more proactive and predictive research and current-awareness workflows, including horizon scanning. He identifies integration with CRM systems and other databases, as well as delivery inside the user's working environment, as essential to supplying contextually useful information to lawyers and business-development staff. These are development directions rather than measured capabilities.
qs: the system will be much more proactive and alerting them at the right time.
And one of the big challenges we’re working on is sort of thinking about that horizon scanning solution.
I may be working in teams. I may be working in the CRM. What type of role have I got in the organization? Where do I want to receive the information?

kp.k: Knowledge teams should become frontline intelligence functions
kp.d: Dickinson describes 'insight activation' as information changing behaviour rather than merely filling inboxes. He says Vable is incorporating GenAI to link disparate publisher and other data and generate first-draft insights. His recommendation is augmentation of professional expertise, with a prediction that firms treating knowledge-management teams as frontline intelligence rather than back-office functions will thrive.
qs: This is happens when content actually becomes or changes behavior, not just fills inbox.
And even generating those insights, I’d like to think sort of first draft insights, because we don’t want to replace humans in this respect.
how firms use AI. to support expertise and decision making, not to replace it.
I think those firms that will thrive will be the ones that stop treating sort of KM teams as back office functions, et cetera, but more so starting to treat them as frontline intelligence.

kp.k: Adoption remains transitional despite higher lawyer expectations
kp.d: Dickinson says both large and small firms still rely substantially on headlines and newsletters. Technical development, adoption and changes to established workflows take time, even when decision-makers support change and lawyers understand more of what is possible. He reports that some firms use Vable Connect for personalised client digests and that lawyers currently add their own commentary to news to initiate client conversations; automating that commentary is an aspiration rather than established practice in his account.
qs: the solutions then need to be adopted by law firms, and there will be impact workflows and ways of working.
for the time being, and there’s an evolutionary phase, and we’re still relying to a large extent on headlines and newsletters.
This allows BD teams to create personalized current awareness for each user in a client organization.
I’m going to use that to then spin that out to a client with my own commentary, the reasons why it’s important. So sort of things which in due course, want AI to be doing.

kp.k: Content rights become part of AI information infrastructure
kp.d: Dickinson reports greater publisher wariness about content use. He describes Vable's response as publisher relationships, connectors, transparency and a rights-intelligence layer identifying provenance, licences and whether GenAI processing is permitted. Article tagging also accompanies API feeds into clients' systems. Publisher portals providing greater visibility are described as an evolving approach, not proof that all permissions issues are resolved.
qs: things have definitely changed a lot and certainly big publishers are more wary about how their content is being used.
Where does this content come from? What can I do with it? Can I run GenAI over it? What license do I have for it?
we’re feeding content to an API into their own system so they can work on that and making sure all articles are tagged up in the right way.
build these sort of publisher portals to give publishers much more visibility over how their content is being used.

kp.k: Ethical current awareness requires four governance pillars
kp.d: Dickinson proposes trust, transparency, accuracy and inclusion as guides for AI alerting, summarisation and filtering. He recommends disclosure of how content is created, filtered and ranked, including AI labelling and access to original sources. Inclusion means avoiding echo chambers through diverse sources, jurisdictions and perspectives. He argues that users disengage when they cannot trust summaries or filters.
qs: If they don’t trust the source summary or filter, they’ll disengage and that undermines the whole purpose of the current awareness.
how it filtered, how it was ranked, and including whether AI was used.
a summary that is clearly labeled as AI generated with the option to view the original source.
The fourth pillar is inclusion.
ensuring that content generated reflects a diversity of sources, jurisdictions, and perspectives.

kp.k: Review intensity should reflect audience and consequences
kp.d: Dickinson suggests that internal alerts may tolerate a lower quality threshold, illustratively 80% accuracy, whereas alerts for senior partners or clients may require a much higher threshold, possibly 100%. These are proposed thresholds, not measured model accuracy rates. He stresses editorial oversight because misleading summaries create legal, reputational and client risks, and says Vable provides administrators with review and curation tools before distribution.
qs: Maybe they need to be the threshold of 80 % accuracy.
if alerts are going to the senior partners or to clients, then threshold is going to be much, much higher, possibly 100%.
And this is where editorial oversight is really critical.
Inaccurate alerts or misleading summaries can create legal, reputational client risk, et cetera.
We say it’s really important and allows for human review before full sending.

kp.k: Predictive AI must support, not replace, professional judgment
kp.d: Dickinson favours using AI to generate starting points and possible implications rather than treating predictions as authoritative. Lawyers must judge and develop those suggestions and retain responsibility for final output and client communication. His account explicitly advocates human-in-the-loop augmentation, not autonomous reliance or delegation of the final professional decision.
qs: it’s mustn’t treated as the oracle.
ultimately, the lawyers have to take what they’re given and make something of it, make their own judgment.
But they’ve got to do the final bit and that’s we must not delegate.
we have to be the ones who are going to take responsibility for the output and the communication with the clients.

kp.k: Controlled sources mitigate fabricated information risks
kp.d: Asked about AI-generated false research entering news feeds, Dickinson describes client-controlled source selection as Vable's mitigation: trusted paid, government and regulatory sources constrain what can enter the system. He acknowledges the trade-off between broad coverage and controlled inputs, and explicitly does not promise perfection. This concerns source selection and provenance, rather than a reported model benchmark or demonstrated error-elimination method.
qs: the way we try and overcome that is, again, it’s about the control over the input, the control over the content.
there’s no black box going on here.
it’s slightly limiting in a way because we’re not saying we’ve got the whole world in there
It won’t be perfect, but my goodness me it’s going to be pretty good.

kp.k: Rapid AI development complicates vendor product planning
kp.d: Dickinson says technological breakthroughs can disrupt nine- or twelve-month projects partway through. He reports that Vable waited somewhat for AI to become more accessible and outlines a six-month plan to begin adding greater personalisation and prediction. Although he experiments with horizon-scanning data and presentation formats, he says the company's priority is decision support rather than visual or audio outputs.
qs: we could start a project which is a nine month, 12 month project and sort of halfway through, there’s another incredible innovation breakthrough.
to a large extent, we’ve waited a little bit until AI has become much more accessible
we’ve got a plan over the next six months
start on that road for making it much more personalized for the end user and start getting more prediction coming into the platform.
our core is to focus on less of the visual and audio, but sticking very much to the core problem at hand, which is helping lawyers make really good decisions with as little effort as possible.

kp.k: Legal technology must accommodate high stakes and practice autonomy
kp.d: Dickinson argues that building for law firms requires understanding their distinctive reliance on information and their internal heterogeneity. Information supports legal advice, partner preparation and reputational-risk identification, raising accuracy demands. Different practice cultures and partner autonomy mean vendors must design around actual lawyer behaviour and earn trust rather than assume uniform workflows.
qs: They operate in high trust, high stakes environments and the margin for error is incredibly small.
the content we deliver isn’t just being read, it’s actually being relied upon is to give legal advice to prepare a partner for a client call or even spot a reputational risk.
Each practice area has its own culture, partners, value, autonomy, et cetera.
thinking about how lawyers work and not about what we wish they did

kp.k: Personalised awareness bots are a speculative future direction
kp.d: In the closing forecast, Dickinson envisages personal current-awareness bots that know users' information needs and supply proactive insights. He grounds his optimism partly in his own experience of doing things he could not do twelve months earlier, not systematic evidence. He emphasises limited foresight beyond six months and conditions the optimistic scenario on people retaining control of important judgments and creativity.
qs: Six months is as far as we can really look in terms of how things are going to change
I think we’re going to end up with our personalized current awareness bot, which knows us, knows what we want in terms of information, provides us with a flawless service, proactive and insightful.
what’s around the corner, I don’t know.
we do need to stay in charge. No delegation of the important things, that creativity or things which are important to us in how we go from A to B.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Matthew Dickinson claims GenAI is shifting legal current awareness from article distribution to personalised, contextual and actionable intelligence.
pts.d: Dickinson says lawyers increasingly expect systems to identify relevance, summarise developments and explain possible implications rather than deliver lists for them to read. His illustrative data-breach scenario connects news to a firm's client and identifies other people in the firm who should know. He predicts more proactive, predictive workflows, including horizon scanning and delivery through systems such as Teams and CRM. These are a mixture of claimed changes in expectations and development ambitions, not a claim that Vable has already implemented every capability.

pts.k: Dickinson presents AI as a way to augment professional judgment and reposition knowledge-management teams, rather than replace human expertise.
pts.d: He says GenAI can link disparate data and generate first-draft insights, giving lawyers starting points from which to exercise judgment. He predicts that firms treating KM teams as frontline intelligence rather than back-office functions will thrive. This is an augmentation argument: lawyers retain responsibility for final judgments and client communications. His insistence on human involvement should not be read as evidence of a measured employment effect or a categorical prediction that no jobs will disappear.

pts.k: Dickinson anticipates AI-assisted client engagement and ultimately individualised current-awareness bots.
pts.d: He describes lawyers currently using news to initiate client conversations with their own commentary, and identifies this as work AI should undertake in due course. Separately, his crystal-ball prediction is that individuals will have personalised current-awareness bots that understand their information needs and provide proactive insights. The promised 'flawless service' is part of that speculative vision, not an observed reliability result.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is Dickinson's vendor experience, reported product development and personal experimentation; no quantified evaluation of AI benefits is supplied.
pts.d: Speaking as Vable's founder and CEO, Dickinson draws on existing aggregation and curation workflows, client practices, planned GenAI functionality and his own use of AI. His data-breach scenario illustrates a desired workflow rather than a documented deployment outcome. Vable Connect is offered as an existing example of personalised client newsletters, not demonstrated AI automation. There are no benchmark results, measured time savings, adoption statistics or comparative outcome studies supporting the predictions. The hosts' court-sanctions discussion and the promotional introduction's quoted productivity claim are not Dickinson's evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Dickinson distinguishes a present transition from a six-month development horizon and more uncertain longer-term possibilities.
pts.d: At the time of the interview, he says both large and small firms still rely substantially on headlines and newsletters. Technical development, adoption and workflow changes must precede the fuller transition. He reports a six-month plan to begin introducing more personalisation and prediction, not to complete the entire vision within that period. Client-outreach automation is an aspiration 'in due course'; personalised bots have no firm delivery date. He explicitly limits confidence in looking beyond roughly six months.

pts.k: The anticipated benefits are conditional on human judgment, trusted inputs, transparency, appropriate review and content-use permissions.
pts.d: Dickinson warns that predictive outputs must not be treated as an oracle. He advocates human review before sending alerts and higher quality requirements for senior-partner or client communications. His references to 80% and 100% accuracy are illustrative desired thresholds, not measured system performance. He claims controlling input sources helps reduce exposure to fabricated material, while acknowledging imperfection. Publisher relationships and a rights-intelligence layer are described as mechanisms for establishing whether content may be processed with GenAI and for making permissions visible.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are lawyers, information professionals, KM and business-development teams, law-firm clients, and publishers.
pts.d: For lawyers, Dickinson anticipates less effort spent reading and triaging news and better starting points for decisions, while preserving responsibility for advice. Librarians and information specialists remain important in selecting sources and curating outputs; KM teams could gain a more strategic intelligence role. BD teams and clients are affected through more personalised awareness and opportunities for relevant outreach. He describes the transition as applying to large and small firms without substantiating a comparative advantage for either. Publishers and Vable, a legal-information technology vendor rather than an ALSP, face requirements for trusted access, licensing transparency and visibility into content use.
